belief: What happened makes me dirty or bad.
origins: This belief often follows sexual abuse, assault, betrayal, or humiliation. Shame can attach itself to the person who was hurt rather than to the person who did the harm. Abusers sometimes tell victims they are dirty or that no one will want them. Religious messages about purity, when misapplied, can deepen the feeling of being stained or ruined.
teaches: In the Gospels, Jesus touched people others considered unclean and said, “Be clean!” He was not made dirty by them; they were made clean by Him. Those who look to the Lord are radiant, and their faces are never covered with shame. God gives a crown of beauty instead of ashes. In Christ, anyone is a new creation, and believers can draw near to God with hearts sprinkled clean. What was done to you does not make you dirty, and nothing you have done is beyond His cleansing.
self_statements: No one would want me if they knew.
I feel dirty no matter what I do.
God must see me as stained.
What happened is who I am now.
errors: Believing I am dirty because I feel dirty.
Calling myself ruined or damaged because of what happened.
Taking on shame that belongs to the person who harmed me.
Letting one experience define my whole identity.
questions: Whose shame am I carrying: mine or the person who hurt me?
Who told me I was dirty or ruined?
How did Jesus treat people others called unclean?
Would I see a friend as dirty if this had happened to her or him?
What does God say about those who look to Him?
What would it mean to see myself as God sees me?
truth: Something painful and wrong happened. The shame belongs to the one who did it, not to me. Jesus is not repelled by me; He reaches out and makes me clean. I am not ruined. In Christ I am a new creation, and my face does not have to be covered with shame.
hw_truths: What was done to me does not make me dirty.
Jesus touches me and says, “Be clean!”
Those who look to Him are radiant.
I am a new creation in Christ.
The shame belongs to the one who harmed me.
log: Each day, write one moment when shame came up, and one truth from this card that answers it.
actions: Write what happened and, next to it, write who is responsible. Then write, “This shame belongs to them, not to me.”
Read how Jesus touched the man with leprosy. Write what it shows you about how Jesus sees you.
Do one kind thing for your body this week, such as a warm bath, rest, or a walk, treating it as something God made good.
Healing from abuse or assault is hard to do alone. A counselor trained in trauma can walk with you at a safe pace.
tracker: A moment I saw myself as clean
prayer: Lord Jesus, I have felt dirty and ruined because of what happened. Thank You that You reached out and touched those others called unclean. Lift my shame, heal my wounds, and help me see myself as You see me: clean, loved, and new. Amen.
